title: Calls for Reform, Global Culture, and Resistance
subject: AP World History

chunks.text: In 1948, in the shadow of WWII and the Holocaust, the United Nations adopted the Universal Declaration of Human Rights. Its thirty articles proclaimed that every human being possesses fundamental rights simply by being human, announcing the powerful new global idea that human rights are universal.

The principle that all people possess equal dignity and rights was rooted in the Enlightenment ideals of liberty and equality but long denied in practice. In the twentieth century it spread and deepened across the globe through overlapping reform movements.

Decolonization was itself a vast assertion of the right of peoples to self-determination, part of the broader twentieth-century expansion of human rights and a model that inspired other movements demanding equality and dignity.

The Civil Rights Movement in the United States and the anti-apartheid struggle in South Africa fought to extend full legal and political equality to people oppressed by racial hierarchies, central chapters in the global expansion of human rights.

The women's rights movement, building on suffrage campaigns that won women the vote in many countries around the world wars, expanded into a global push for equality in education, work, politics, family law, and bodily autonomy, transforming the status of half of humanity, though unevenly across regions.

Reform movements shared common ideals — equality, dignity, self-determination, and universal human rights — and inspired and borrowed tactics from one another across borders, as Gandhi's methods inspired the American civil rights movement, which in turn inspired movements worldwide.

As goods, media, and people moved across the world, a shared global culture emerged: Hollywood films, popular music, global sports like soccer, fashion, fast food, and internet media created common cultural references shared by billions.

Because much global culture originated in the wealthy West, especially the United States, critics describe parts of it as 'Americanization' and fear cultural homogenization — that a single commercialized global monoculture is erasing the world's diversity of local traditions, languages, and ways of life.

Rather than one culture simply replacing all others, globalization often produced cultural blending and adaptation (hybridization), as people combined global products and ideas with local traditions to create something new, selecting and reinterpreting global culture rather than passively absorbing it.

Cultures have always blended through exchange, a continuity stretching back to the Silk Roads and earlier networks. Globalization accelerated this ancient process rather than inventing it, producing new hybrid forms of music, food, fashion, and ideas.

The spread of global culture provoked powerful resistance and backlash. Many people experienced global culture as a threat to their identity, religion, values, or traditional ways of life, and responded by reasserting and defending the local.

The defining cultural dynamic of the global age is not simply homogenization but a constant tension between the global and the local — between integration and the determined defense of difference, expressed through spread, blending, and resistance.

Religious fundamentalism, a global phenomenon across many of the world's religions in the late twentieth century, called for a return to fundamental traditional truths of faith, often rejecting aspects of modern, secular, globalized society.

Religious fundamentalism grew in the age of globalization because rapid change felt destabilizing: as global culture, secular values, and economic disruption swept in, many people lost identity, community, and meaning. Fundamentalism offered clear identity, community, and certainty, making it a distinctly modern reaction to modern conditions.

Resistance to globalization took many forms: religious fundamentalism, a resurgence of nationalism, movements to protect local languages and customs, and organized anti-globalization protest opposing free trade and corporate power.

Resistance to globalization should be analyzed by its causes — perceived threats to identity, religion, or values; economic hardship and inequality; resentment of Western or corporate dominance; loss of community and meaning — not dismissed as irrational or marginal.

Three cultural responses to globalization can be distinguished: spread/homogenization (shared global culture spreads worldwide), blending/hybridization (global and local combine into new forms), and resistance/backlash (reasserting local identity against global culture).

The expansion of human rights in the twentieth century was real and historic but remained incomplete and contested, representing globalization at its most hopeful: the worldwide spread not just of goods but of the idea that every human being matters.

Faced with globalization, people were not passive: they used its universal ideals to demand rights long denied, creatively blended global and local to make new cultures, and resisted when they felt their identities and ways of life were threatened. The global age is a dynamic, contested encounter between global and local.

The backlash against globalization — religious, nationalist, and anti-globalization — is one of the defining political forces of the present day, shaping elections, conflicts, and movements across the contemporary world.

Analyzing reactions to change requires identifying the change being reacted to, explaining the causes of the reaction, categorizing responses as reform, adaptation/blending, or resistance, and connecting the specific reaction to the broader tension between the global and the local.
